meta.title: Banking, ESG and financial regulation, 16 days of posts
meta.subject: financial services policy in Texas — the anti-ESG and anti-boycott laws covering energy and firearms, the Comptroller's lists of boycotting firms, state banking and lending law, the Department of Banking, the Texas Stock Exchange and Texas as a financial center, and bank fees and consumer finance rules
meta.subtitle: Oct 1 to Oct 16, 2026. Each dot is one post with 1K+ views about Texas banking, ESG and financial regulation, plus every post repeating an earlier one, in the lane for what it argues. Higher and bigger means more views. White means 90% or more the same words as an earlier post, with a white line back to it. Coloured lines link a post to the post it quoted or replied to. Updated daily.

lanes.label: Companies fleeing NY for Texas
lanes.description: Corporate headquarters, capital and financial talent are relocating from New York and California to Dallas, Austin and Houston, so Texas is pulling the financial center of gravity away from Wall Street.

lanes.label: Texas Stock Exchange as rival
lanes.description: The Dallas-based Texas Stock Exchange is a credible challenger to the NYSE and Nasdaq, built to give companies a business-friendly listing venue and cement Texas as a financial center.

lanes.label: Woke capital vs free markets
lanes.description: Anti-ESG and anti-boycott laws stop woke banks and asset managers from using ESG, climate and gun-control agendas to punish Texas oil, gas and firearms industries.

lanes.label: Comptroller's boycott blacklist enforcement
lanes.description: The Comptroller's lists of boycotting financial firms are an accountability tool that bars named firms from state contracts, and critics say they are arbitrary or politically motivated.

lanes.label: Boycott laws raise costs
lanes.description: Critics argue that excluding banks under the boycott laws raises borrowing costs for Texas cities and taxpayers, shrinks competition for municipal bonds and hurts the state's financial standing.

lanes.label: Bank fees and consumer protections
lanes.description: Posts about bank fees, lending rules and Department of Banking oversight argue over whether Texas law protects or fails consumers, including debanking, overdraft and junk fees.

lanes.label: Pushback
lanes.description: Posts doubting, mocking, fact-checking or arguing against the dominant framings.

posts.name: Fox News Politics
posts.text:
Texas is pulling the financial center of gravity away from New York — and the numbers back it up.

Dallas-Fort Worth has led the entire nation with 111 corporate headquarters relocations since 2018, followed by Austin with 88 and Houston with 31, according to CBRE data. Companies are citing growth opportunities, lower operating costs, and lighter regulation.

Now the Texas Stock Exchange, which received SEC approval last year, is gunning directly for the NYSE and Nasdaq. It already has primary listings from Energy Transfer, Dillard's, Sunoco, and Texas Capital Bank — with backing from JPMorgan and BlackRock. Former Congressman Jeb Hensarling, a board member, says the exchange is the final piece of a transformation that's been building for years: "Texas has been a great place to do business for decades. But increasingly, it's a great place to headquarter your business... And really the last piece of that puzzle was the Texas Stock Exchange."

Full story here https://t.co/GVffWuJ2A4

posts.name: Marc Gravely
posts.text:
Morgan Stanley just picked Dallas for more than 3,800 new jobs.

JPMorgan, the bank it split from in 1935, already employs more people in Texas than in New York.

On September 28, Morgan Stanley confirmed a new US hub in Dallas: $684 million invested and more than 3,800 jobs by 2035.

It starts in about 255,000 square feet at Fountain Place downtown. Around 2031 it moves into a new 700,000 square foot campus in Uptown.

The state is putting in a $43.8 million Texas Enterprise Fund grant, and the city has its own incentive package.

The jobs won't arrive all at once. About 1,500 are expected by 2031, the rest by 2035.

But Dallas didn't come out of nowhere, and the story starts in New York:

In 1933, the Glass-Steagall Act made banks choose between taking deposits and selling securities. J.P. Morgan & Co. kept the deposits. In 1935, Henry Morgan and Harold Stanley left to start Morgan Stanley.

By 2024, JPMorgan Chase had 31,500 employees in Texas. That's more than it had in New York, and more than in any other state.

It has more than 17,000 in North Texas alone. Goldman Sachs, Charles Schwab, Fidelity, Wells Fargo and Citi are all in DFW, and so is the new Texas Stock Exchange.

DFW now holds 41% of the state's financial services jobs, with 27% of its people.

A law in Washington split the House of Morgan in two. Ninety-one years later, both halves are hiring in Dallas.

posts.name: Rare DD
posts.text:
Formerly of the @SECGov's Division of Trading and Markets, David Saltiel’s position and movements carry distinct institutional significance when evaluated through the lens of market structure oversight and regulatory interactions...

Direct Authority Over Market Mechanics: 

As a high-ranking official (serving as Deputy Director, Associate Director of the Office of Analytics and Research, and twice as Acting Director) within the Division of Trading and Markets, Saltiel sat at the exact regulatory intersection responsible for broker-dealer practices, clearing and settlement operational rules, and market surveillance systems.

Proximity to Critical Turning Points: 

His inclusion in the December 2022 communications right before FINRA’s MMTLP symbol deletion, followed by direct engagement with broker-dealer lobbying groups (like the Financial Information Forum) regarding post-halt S-1 filings and unrecovered stock loans in late 2023, places him directly inside the administrative loop managing the fallout of the MMTLP/Next Bridge situation.   

The "Revolving Door" Dynamic:

Saltiel's departure from the SEC to take on a senior leadership role at the Texas Stock Exchange (TXSE), an institution backed by major market-making entities and financial heavyweights like Citadel Securities highlights a pattern frequently criticized by market observers. Moving from a key regulatory seat governing market structure and clearing oversight directly into an exchange ecosystem funded by major industry participants underscores the close ties between regulators and the private financial entities they oversee.

The "Bad Optics" of Regulatory Timing:

When officials intimately involved in contested market events—such as handling broker-dealer fallout, disputed corporate filings, or communication loops with self-regulatory bodies—exit the agency right as administrative control shifts, it reinforces public skepticism. Even if routine career moves or political changes motivate individual exits, the proximity to unresolved structural controversies makes it look like accountability is being evaded, leaving outside observers with the impression of an agency closing ranks.
